The words you need for [the Everyday Tonality lessons](tagg-sound.qmd), in Tagg's sense (he avoids some school words on purpose: *ionian* instead of *major*, *tonical* for 'to do with the home note'). Each ends with the book page it comes from.

## A

**aeolian shuttle**: A shuttle between a minor home chord and the major chord on the flat sixth note. It is often linked to ominous, cold or waiting moods. (Tagg p. 386)

**anacrusis**: A short lead-in or pickup that pushes the music into the next chord. It helps show which chord is home. (Tagg pp. 429, 448)

## B

**bimodal**: Music that can be heard in two modes, so that two chords can each sound like the tonic. (Tagg pp. 436, 449–450)

## C

**chord loop**: A short chord pattern of three or four chords that repeats. It gives groove and a steady tonal motor, not a long story. (Tagg p. 275)

**chord shuttle**: A pattern that swings back and forth between two chords, with about equal time on each. It is short enough to be heard as one "now". (Tagg p. 371)

**circle of fifths (key clock)**: A diagram of the twelve keys as a clock, with each step a fifth apart. Moving clockwise adds sharps and moving anticlockwise adds flats. (Tagg pp. 255–256)

**classical harmony**: Tagg's name for the chord habits of European art music from about 1700 to 1900, built on stacked thirds, the major scale and V–I endings. It spread worldwide but is only one style among many. (Tagg p. 249)

**Counterpoint**: Polyphony in which the lines clearly differ in melody and/or rhythm. It is the opposite of homophony, though music is only more or less contrapuntal. (Tagg p. 214–215)

**counterpoise**: The "tonal elsewhere": a second pole that a tune moves to and back from, apart from its tonic. It is often found in drone-based folk music. (Tagg p. 336)

## D

**Doh-pentatonic**: The five-note mode that centres on doh; it is the "major pentatonic" and is the only one of the five with a major third. Amazing Grace is an example. (Tagg p. 155, 177)

**Drone**: A note that sounds at the same pitch throughout all or part of a piece, acting as a reference for the other parts; bagpipes are the classic example. (Tagg p. 207–208)

## E

**equal temperament**: The tuning that splits the octave into 12 equal semitones. It is used on pianos and keyboards, but it slightly changes the "pure" intervals. (Tagg p. 74)

**extended present**: A stretch of time (a few seconds) that we hear as one unit, "now". Tagg says a shuttle or a simple loop fits inside it. (Tagg p. 371)

## H

**Hexatonic**: A mode with six different notes per octave, such as the seventhless doh-hexatonic or the sixthless la-hexatonic. (Tagg p. 165–166)

**Homophony**: Polyphony where the parts move in the same rhythm at the same time, like a hymn. (Tagg p. 212)

## I

**interval**: The distance in pitch between two tones. We measure it in semitones or in cents (100 cents = 1 semitone). (Tagg p. 67)

**IOCM (interobjective comparison material)**: Other music that sounds like or is built like the piece you are studying. It helps you work out what the piece means. (Tagg p. 452)

**ionian**: Tagg's word for the major scale. He avoids calling it the default or "normal", because it is only one mode among many. (Tagg p. 90)

**ionianisation**: The classical habit of treating the ionian mode as the norm, and bending other modes (such as minor) to fit it, for example by raising the seventh note. (Tagg p. 90)

## L

**La-pentatonic**: The five-note mode that centres on la; it is the "minor pentatonic" and is used all over rock music. The blues version adds a flat five. (Tagg p. 156, 161)

**Lead sheet**: A page with the melody, chord symbols and lyrics of a song; the chord symbols are called lead-sheet chord shorthand and name chords in absolute terms (C, Dm7, G7). (Tagg p. 229–230)

**leading note**: A note that pulls to the note a semitone away. In the major scale the seventh pulls up to the home note and the fourth pulls down to the third. (Tagg p. 253)

## M

**maqam**: The Arab idea of a mode, with extra rules about which notes to stress and how a melody should move. The octave is thought of as two tetrachords. (Tagg p. 114)

**Melisma**: Several smooth, joined notes sung to one syllable. It is the opposite of syllabic singing (one note per syllable) and is heard as emotional. (Tagg p. 199)

**milksap**: Tagg's word for the bland teen pop of about 1957 to 1963, built on the I–vi–IV–V vamp. (Tagg pp. 407, 411)

**mixolydian shuttle**: A shuttle between the home chord and the major chord a whole step below it (I and bVII). It is common in intros and linked to waiting. (Tagg pp. 389, 391)

**mode**: A tonal vocabulary reduced to one occurrence of each note, put in order inside one octave. The major scale is one mode (the ionian). (Tagg p. 86)

## N

**note**: One single sound that starts and ends. It can be high or low, or even have no clear pitch, like a drum hit. (Tagg p. 45)

## O

**Octatonic scale**: An eight-note scale of alternating whole tones and semitones; film uses it for mystery and jazz players call it the "diminished scale". (Tagg p. 175)

**octave**: The interval between two notes where the top one vibrates twice as fast as the bottom. Cultures treat them as the same note in two registers. (Tagg p. 68)

**one-chord change**: A "single" chord on a chord sheet which in practice is played as two or more chords moving in a loop, such as G, C over D, G. (Tagg pp. 353, 367, 369)

## P

**Pentatonic**: A mode with five different notes per octave. Anhemitonic pentatonic modes have no semitones and can be played on the black keys of a piano. (Tagg p. 151, 153)

**perfect cadence**: A V–I chord ending, the strongest "finished" sound in classical harmony. Tagg says the other cadence names (half, plagal, interrupted) reflect classical habits. (Tagg pp. 252, 258–261)

**Picardy third**: A major third in a tonic chord of a minor piece. Normally used only at the end, but many non-classical styles use it throughout. (Tagg pp. 276–277)

**pitch**: How high or low a sound is. It comes from how fast the sound vibrates, measured in hertz (Hz). (Tagg p. 47)

**Pitch contour**: The overall shape a melody draws as it goes up and down, for example rising, falling, arched or wavy. (Tagg p. 183)

**place to be**: Tagg's name for a shuttle or loop that is a lasting mood, not a path leading somewhere. (Tagg p. 379)

**plagal cadence**: A IV–I ending, like the "Amen" at the end of a hymn. (Tagg p. 259)

**plagal shuttle**: A shuttle between a chord and the chord a fourth above it, such as D and G. It is very common in pop and rock. (Tagg pp. 375, 399)

**Polyphony**: Music in which two or more sounds, or in the tonal sense two or more different pitches, are heard at the same time. (Tagg p. 205–206)

**power chord**: A two-note chord (root and fifth) played on a distorted electric guitar. Distortion adds overtones, including a major third, so it sounds full and stable. (Tagg p. 280)

## Q

**Quartal**: Mode or chord without a third; a "quartal" mode such as ré-pentatonic is neither major nor minor. (Tagg p. 166, 178)

**quartal**: Describes chords built by stacking fourths (or fifths, the upside-down version). Their sound and logic differ from stacked-thirds chords. (Tagg pp. 250, 295)

## R

**Ré-pentatonic**: A five-note mode centring on ré that has neither a major nor a minor third, so it is often wrongly heard as dorian. (Tagg p. 156–157)

## S

**scale degree**: A note's number in a mode, counted from the tonic as 1. A flat sign before the number means one semitone lower than in the ionian mode. (Tagg p. 32)

## T

**Tertial**: Describes chords built by stacking thirds, as in common major and minor triads. It is different from quartal harmony, built on fourths. (Tagg p. 219–220)

**tertial**: Describes chords made by stacking thirds. Tagg uses it so that "triad", which only means a three-note chord, is not confused with chords built from thirds. (Tagg pp. 250–251)

**timbre**: The sound quality that lets you tell two instruments apart even when they play the same pitch at the same volume. It comes from the attack, sustain, release and mix of overtones. (Tagg p. 58)

**tonal**: Made of tones, or having the qualities of a tone. Tagg uses it for all music with pitched notes, not just classical music. (Tagg p. 51)

**tonality**: The system a music culture uses to organise its tones. Every culture has its own, so there is more than one. (Tagg p. 56)

**tone**: A note with a pitch you can clearly hear. A hi-hat is a note but not a tone. (Tagg p. 51)

**tonic**: The home note or keynote that a piece or section is built around. Music with a tonic is "tonical". (Tagg p. 57)

**tonical neighbourhood**: The area of nearby notes on the key clock that a quartal chord covers. Music can shift within it without feeling like a key change. (Tagg pp. 297, 299)

**triad**: Any chord with three differently named notes, whether built from thirds or not. (Tagg p. 251)

**turnaround**: A short chord sequence at the end of a section that leads back to the start. Some turnarounds can also be used as loops. (Tagg pp. 402, 411)

## U

**unidirectional**: Going one way only. A "unidirectional" progression, like ii–V–I, heads in one direction towards a goal, unlike a shuttle that swings back and forth. (Tagg p. 377)

## V

**vamp**: A chord sequence of the type I–vi–ii–V (or I–vi–IV–V), with the roots falling by fifths. It comes from jazz standards and musicals. (Tagg pp. 404, 419)

**voice leading**: How each note in one chord moves to a note in the next. Classical harmony has rules about this, for example that sevenths fall and leading notes rise. (Tagg pp. 252, 271)

## W

**Whole-tone scale**: A six-note scale made of whole tones only; it has no perfect fifth or fourth, so it sounds unrooted and is used for dream or mystery scenes. (Tagg p. 173–174)
